claim: The sense of ownership of one's body is important for survival, e.g., in defending the body against a threat.
source: The sense of ownership of one's body is important for survival, e.g., in defending the body against a threat.
evidence: This is a general statement about body ownership based on established understanding in the field.

claim: The sense of ownership causes external space to be perceptually scaled according to the size of the body.
source: In the case of visuospatial perception, it has been shown that the sense of ownership causes external space to be perceptually scaled according to the size of the body.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research in the field.

claim: Ownership, but not mere visuotactile stimulation, increases the dominance of the hand percept in binocular rivalry.
source: The results show that ownership, but not mere visuotactile stimulation, increases the dominance of the hand percept.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of ownership on hand percept dominance is due to a combination of longer perceptual dominance durations and shorter suppression durations.
source: This effect is due to a combination of longer perceptual dominance durations and shorter suppression durations.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The sense of body ownership promotes visual awareness.
source: Together, these results suggest that the sense of body ownership promotes visual awareness.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Visual awareness of one's body occurs without exerting any effort upon opening one's eyes and looking down.
source: Upon opening one's eyes and looking down at one's body, one becomes visually aware of one's hands, legs, and chest without exerting any effort.
evidence: This is a phenomenological observation based on common experience.

claim: The feeling of body ownership distinguishes one's own body from external objects.
source: The feeling of body ownership distinguishes one's own body from external objects; this distinction is critical, for example, when an external object threatens the body.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim about the function of body ownership.

claim: One's own body can be assumed to be more relevant than any other object.
source: Because one's own body can be assumed to be more relevant than any other object, it is reasonable to expect that visual awareness will be boosted when, all else being equal, body ownership is present.
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption underlying the study's hypothesis.

claim: In the rubber-hand illusion, participants experience ownership of an external object (a rubber hand).
source: However, in the classic rubber-hand illusion, participants do experience ownership of an external object, namely, a rubber hand that is in front of them (Botvinick and Cohen, 1998).
evidence: This is a well-established finding from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: After synchronous brushing of the rubber hand and the participant's real hand, the participant reports a sensation of ownership of the rubber hand.
source: After synchronous brushing of the rubber hand and the participant's real hand for a short period, the participant reports a sensation of ownership of the rubber hand and perceives that tactile sensations originate from the rubber hand.
evidence: This describes the classic rubber-hand illusion procedure and outcome, supported by citation.

claim: For ownership of an artificial hand to be induced, the hand must be placed in the same orientation as the real hand.
source: For example, these studies have shown that for ownership of an artificial hand to be induced, the hand must be placed in the same orientation as the real hand, and visuotactile stimulation applied to the rubber hand must be synchronously applied in the same direction as that applied to the veridical hand (Makin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: The rubber-hand illusion is a multisensory illusion.
source: From this line of research, it is clear that the rubber-hand illusion is a multisensory illusion (Ehrsson, 2012; Graziano and Botvinick, 2002; Tsakiris, 2010)
evidence: This is a conclusion from prior research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ownership of limbs and full bodies depends on the dynamic integration of spatially and temporally congruent visual, tactile and proprioceptive information from a space near the body.
source: and that ownership of limbs (Makin et al., 2008) and full bodies (Blanke et al., 2015; Ehrsson, 2012; Petkova and Ehrsson, 2008) depends on the dynamic integration of spatially and temporally congruent visual, tactile and proprioceptive information from a space near the body.
evidence: This is a finding from prior research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Body ownership plays an important role in visual perception, affecting how one sees the external world beyond one's body.
source: Recent studies have also shown that body ownership plays an important role in visual perception more generally, affecting how one sees the external world beyond one's body (Banakou et al., 2013; Haggard and Jundi, 2009; Linkenauger et al., 2013; van der Hoort et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from prior research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Body size serves as a ruler in the size perception of objects in the external world, but only in the presence of ownership.
source: In particular, studies have shown that body size serves as a ruler in the size perception of objects in the external world, but only in the presence of ownership (van der Hoort and Ehrsson, 2014, van der Hoort and Ehrsson, 2016; van der Hoort et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from prior research, supported by citations.

claim: When participants experience body ownership of a small doll, other objects appear larger and farther away.
source: When participants experience body ownership of a small doll, other objects appear larger and farther away; conversely, ownership of a large artificial body makes other objects appear smaller and closer.
evidence: This is a finding from prior research on body ownership and size perception.

claim: When ownership is disrupted, the effects of body size on object perception are greatly diminished, although the visual stimuli are identical.
source: Crucially, when ownership is disrupted, these effects are greatly diminished, although the visual stimuli are identical in the ownership and no-ownership conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from prior research demonstrating the specific role of ownership.

claim: Body ownership appears to have a direct effect on the content of conscious visual perception that cannot be explained by differences in visual input.
source: Thus, body ownership appears to have a direct effect on the content of conscious visual perception that cannot be explained by differences in visual input.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior research findings.

claim: In binocular rivalry, the two eyes are presented with different visual images that compete for visual awareness, resulting in alternating subjective percepts.
source: In binocular rivalry, the two eyes are presented with different visual images that compete for visual awareness, thus resulting in alternating subjective percepts (Levelt, 1965).
evidence: This is a description of the binocular rivalry phenomenon, supported by citation.

claim: Visual parameters such as contrast, spatial frequency, color, and motion together determine the 'stimulus strength' of each of the rival stimuli.
source: Visual parameters such as contrast, spatial frequency, color, and motion together determine the 'stimulus strength' of each of the rival stimuli (Brascamp et al., 2015; Levelt, 1965).
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular rivalry, supported by citations.

claim: Increasing the strength of both stimuli equally increases the switching rate during rivalry.
source: Increasing the strength of both stimuli equally increases the switching rate during rivalry, whereas increasing the strength of only one of the rival stimuli increases the overall perceptual dominance of that stimulus (Brascamp et al., 2015; Levelt, 1965).
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular rivalry dynamics, supported by citations.

claim: Increasing the strength of only one of the rival stimuli increases the overall perceptual dominance of that stimulus.
source: Increasing the strength of both stimuli equally increases the switching rate during rivalry, whereas increasing the strength of only one of the rival stimuli increases the overall perceptual dominance of that stimulus (Brascamp et al., 2015; Levelt, 1965).
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular rivalry dynamics, supported by citations.

claim: Visual awareness of a hand for which ownership is experienced should be prioritized because one's own hand is a more relevant object for the brain to process.
source: We hypothesized that because one's own hand is a more relevant object for the brain to process, visual awareness of a hand for which ownership is experienced should be prioritized.
evidence: This is the hypothesis of the study, based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: The overall dominance of the hand image would increase through the feeling of ownership of the hand.
source: We hypothesized that the overall dominance of the hand image would increase through the feeling of ownership of the hand.
evidence: This is the specific hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: A total of 60 healthy volunteers were tested, equally divided between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2.
source: We tested a total of 60 healthy volunteers, who were equally divided between Experiment 1 (mean age = 24.6; 18 women) and Experiment 2 (mean age = 26.2, 13 women), and who were naive to the purpose of the study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: The number of participants for each experiment (N = 30) was based on previous studies in which body ownership was manipulated.
source: The number of participants for each experiment (N = 30) was based on previous studies in which body ownership was manipulated to investigate its effect on another variable of interest and to allow for correlation analyses (Gentile et al., 2013; Guterstam et al., 2011; Kalckert and Ehrsson, 2012).
evidence: This explains the rationale for sample size, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Nineteen participants out of 30 reported ratings of at least +1 on questionnaire statement Q1 in Experiment 1.
source: Nineteen participants out of the total group of 30 reported ratings of at least +1 on questionnaire statement Q1 ('It felt as if the hand I saw was my own hand'), and the median response was +1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct report of questionnaire data from Experiment 1.

claim: Twenty-three participants reported ratings of at least +1 on Q2 in Experiment 1, with a median of +2.
source: In addition, 23 participants reported ratings of at least +1 on Q2 ('The touch I felt seemed to be caused by the white ball I saw'), and the median was +2.
evidence: This is a direct report of questionnaire data from Experiment 1.

claim: The proportions of participants affirming the illusion-related statements and the median scores are comparable to previous experiments with the rubber hand illusion.
source: These proportions of participants affirming the illusion-related statements and the median scores are comparable to previous experiments with the rubber hand illusion (Kalckert and Ehrsson, 2014).
evidence: This compares the current results to prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Participants rated the illusion statements significantly higher than the control statements in Experiment 1.
source: Crucially, participants rated the illusion statements significantly higher than the control statements (Z = 4.44, p <0.001, r = 0.57).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the questionnaire data analysis.

claim: Ownership of the hand was successfully induced during the visuotactile condition in Experiment 1.
source: Thus, on a group level, these questionnaire results suggest ownership of the hand was successfully induced during the visuotactile condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the questionnaire data.

claim: During the visuotactile condition in Experiment 1, participants observed the hand 43.6% of the time.
source: During the visuotactile condition, in which participants experienced ownership of the hand, participants observed the hand 43.6% of the time, which was more than in any other condition (baseline = 33.9%, no-stimulation = 34.5%, tactile-only = 36.5%, visual-only = 39.1%).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: The overall dominance of the hand was significantly larger in the visuotactile condition compared to the visual only condition in Experiment 1.
source: Planned comparison revealed that the overall dominance of the hand was significantly larger in the visuotactile condition compared to the visual only condition (mean difference ± SEM = 4.48 ± 1.76, CI = 0.87–8.08, t(29) = 2.54, p = 0.017, d = 0.47).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: The hand percept was not more dominant in the tactile-only condition than in the no-stimulation condition in Experiment 1.
source: Interestingly, the hand percept was not more dominant in the tactile-only condition than in the no-stimulation condition as revealed by our planned comparison (mean difference ± SEM = 2.02 ± 2.04, CI = −2.15–6.19, t(29) = 1.30, p = 0.204, d = 0.18).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: It is ownership of the hand, rather than mere tactile stimulation, that increases hand-percept dominance.
source: This result suggests that it is ownership of the hand, rather than mere tactile stimulation, that increases hand-percept dominance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The dominance of the hand percept was similar in the no-stimulation condition and the baseline condition in Experiment 1.
source: The dominance of the hand percept was similar in both conditions (mean difference ± SEM = 0.61 ± 2.22, CI = −3.94–5.15, t(29) = 0.27, p > 0.25, d = 0.05), thus indicating that the mere congruent position of a participant's veridical hand did not increase the dominance of the hand image.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: The mere congruent position of a participant's veridical hand did not increase the dominance of the hand image.
source: The dominance of the hand percept was similar in both conditions (mean difference ± SEM = 0.61 ± 2.22, CI = −3.94–5.15, t(29) = 0.27, p > 0.25, d = 0.05), thus indicating that the mere congruent position of a participant's veridical hand did not increase the dominance of the hand image.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis.

claim: Participants with higher ownership illusion scores had stronger effects on hand dominance in the visuotactile condition in Experiment 1.
source: In a post hoc correlation analysis, we found that participants with higher ownership illusion scores had stronger effects on hand dominance in the visuotactile condition (ρS = 0.53, p = 0.003) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis.

claim: The resulting ownership of the observed hand, rather than mere visuotactile stimulation, caused the increase in the dominance of the hand image.
source: This finding suggests that the resulting ownership of the observed hand, rather than mere visuotactile stimulation, caused the increase in the dominance of the hand image.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: The presence of the moving object in the visuotactile and visual-only conditions changed the overall switching rate in Experiment 1.
source: The presence of the moving object in the visuotactile and visual-only conditions changed the overall switching rate, that is, we found a main effect of the visual component of touch on the switch rate (F(1,29) = 39.97, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.58) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: No differences in switch rate were found between conditions with matched visual stimuli in Experiment 1.
source: but we found no differences between conditions with matched visual stimuli (visuotactile versus visual-only: mean difference ± SEM = 0.018 ± 0.015, CI = 0.045–0.106, t(29) = 1.25, p = 0.221, d = 0.23; tactile-only versus no-stimulation: mean difference ± SEM = 0.001 ± 0.018, CI = −0.029–0.044, t(29) = 0.435, p = 0.667, d = 0.10).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: The visuotactile condition tended to increase the durations of the hand percept compared with the visual-only condition in Experiment 1.
source: After normalizing the mean durations, we found that the visuotactile condition tended to increase the durations of the hand percept compared with the visual-only condition (mean difference ± SEM = 0.092 ± 0.046, CI = −0.003–0.044, t(29) = 1.98, p = 0.057, d = 0.36) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: The durations of suppression were significantly shorter in the visuotactile condition than in the visual-only condition in Experiment 1.
source: In addition, the durations of suppression were significantly shorter in the visuotactile condition than in the visual-only condition (mean difference ± SEM = −1.01 ± 0.046, CI = −0.194 – −0.007, t(29) = −2.21, p = 0.035, d = 0.40).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: The increased overall dominance of the hand image appears to be driven by a combination of prolonged hand percepts and shortened mask percepts.
source: Thus, the increased overall dominance of the hand image appears to be driven by a combination of prolonged hand percepts and shortened mask percepts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the percept duration analysis.

claim: Changes in percept duration appear to be specific to visuotactile stimulation because tactile stimulation without a congruent visual component of touch did not significantly change percept durations.
source: Furthermore, these changes in percept duration appear to be specific to visuotactile stimulation because tactile stimulation without a congruent visual component of touch did not significantly change percept durations compared with those in the no-stimulation condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing different experimental conditions.

claim: For the visuotactile condition in Experiment 1, there was a strong effect of time regarding individual touches on hand dominance.
source: For the visuotactile condition, there was a strong effect of time regarding individual touches (F(5,145) = 35.46, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.55).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the time-course analysis.

claim: Individual touches did not affect dominance in the tactile-only condition in Experiment 1.
source: Surprisingly, individual touches did not affect dominance in the tactile-only condition (F(5,145) = 1.40, p = 0.227, η2 = 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the time-course analysis.

claim: The onset of tactile stimulation did not significantly increase hand dominance.
source: Thus, the onset of tactile stimulation did not significantly increase hand dominance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-course analysis.

claim: The effect of the visuotactile condition seems largest before the onset of a touch, consistent with a continuing ownership effect.
source: In contrast, after visual input and tactile stimulation are controlled for, the effect of the visuotactile condition seems largest before the onset of a touch, a result consistent with a continuing ownership effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the time-course analysis results.

claim: Ownership of a hand, a continuous experience, but not the visual or tactile component of touch alone, increases the overall dominance of that hand in the visuotactile condition.
source: These findings provide additional evidence that ownership of a hand, a continuous experience, but not the visual or tactile component of touch alone, increases the overall dominance of that hand in the visuotactile condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-course analysis results.

claim: The probability of maintaining a hand percept was higher overall during a touch than before a touch in Experiment 1.
source: The probability of maintaining a hand percept was higher overall during a touch than before a touch (F(1,29) = 23.83, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.45).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the single percept analysis.

claim: The visuotactile condition had a tendency toward higher overall probabilities of maintaining a hand percept in Experiment 1.
source: Furthermore, we found that the visuotactile condition had a tendency toward higher overall probabilities of maintaining a hand percept (F(1,29) = 3.21, p = 0.084, η2 = 0.10).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the single percept analysis.

claim: Maintaining the hand percept was more likely in the visuotactile condition, but this effect did not rely on individual touches.
source: Thus, maintaining the hand percept was more likely in the visuotactile condition, but this effect did not rely on individual touches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single percept analysis.

claim: If the hand was suppressed, it was overall more likely to switch to dominance in the visuotactile condition than in the visual-only condition in Experiment 1.
source: We found that if the hand was suppressed, it was overall more likely to switch to dominance in the visuotactile condition than in the visual-only condition (F(1,29) = 4.60, p = 0.046, η2 = 0.14).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the single percept analysis.

claim: The likelihood of recovering a hand percept from suppression was greater in the visuotactile condition, and there was no significant change in this effect during touches.
source: Thus, the likelihood of recovering a hand percept from suppression was greater in the visuotactile condition, and there was no significant change in this effect during touches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single percept analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, the ratings for Q1 and Q2 were significantly higher in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition.
source: The ratings for Q1 and Q2 were significantly higher in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition (Q1: Z = 3.13, p = 0.002, r = 0.40; Q2: Z = 2.36, p = 0.018, r = 0.30), whereas there were no differences for the control statements (Q3: Z = −0.59, p = 0.557, r = 0.08; Q4: Z = 1.73, p = 0.173, r = 0.22).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the questionnaire data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The illusion score was significantly higher in the congruent visuotactile condition than in the incongruent condition in Experiment 2.
source: In accordance with this, the illusion score was significantly higher in the congruent visuotactile condition than in the incongruent condition (Z = 2.73, p < 0.006, r = 0.35).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the questionnaire data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The experimental manipulation of ownership was successful in Experiment 2.
source: Thus, the experimental manipulation of ownership was successful.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the questionnaire data of Experiment 2.

claim: The overall dominance of the hand image was higher in the congruent visuotactile condition than in the congruent visual-only condition in Experiment 2.
source: Planned comparisons showed that the overall dominance of the hand image was higher in the congruent visuotactile condition (mean = 39.9%) than in the congruent visual-only condition (35.6%) (mean difference ± SEM = 4.28 ± 1.16, CI = 1.90–6.65, t(29) = 3.68, p < 0.001, d = 0.68)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: No difference in hand dominance was observed for the incongruent conditions in Experiment 2.
source: but no such difference in hand dominance was observed for the incongruent conditions (visuotactile = 36.5%, visual-only = 36.4%, mean difference = 0.06 ± 1.40, CI = −2,92–2.80, t(29) = 0.04, p = 0.97, d = 0.01) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Mere spatial congruency did not increase the dominance of the hand percept in Experiment 2.
source: Thus, mere spatial congruency did not increase the dominance of the hand percept.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The interaction effect between visuotactile stimulation and congruency was significant in Experiment 2.
source: Crucially, the interaction effect between visuotactile stimulation and congruency was significant (F(1,29) = 6.63, p = 0.015, η2 = 0.19).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Visuotactile stimulation has an effect on dominance only if the hand is in a congruent position.
source: This result indicates that visuotactile stimulation has an effect on dominance only if the hand is in a congruent position.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the interaction effect in Experiment 2.

claim: Dominance is increased by the resulting body ownership and not by the visuotactile stimulation itself.
source: Therefore, these results suggest that dominance is increased by the resulting body ownership and not by the visuotactile stimulation itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 2.

claim: No effect of congruency on the switch rate was found in Experiment 2.
source: We found no effect of congruency on the switch rate (F(1,29) = 0.62, p = 0.437, η2 = 0.02) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Participants had similar switch rates in all four conditions of Experiment 2.
source: Thus, participants had similar switch rates in all four conditions, indicating that the conditions were well matched in terms of perceptual stability of the visual stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the switch rate analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Individual hand percepts lasted longer in the congruent visuotactile condition than in the congruent visual-only condition in Experiment 2.
source: As in Experiment 1, individual hand percepts lasted longer in the congruent visuotactile condition than in the congruent visual-only condition (mean difference ± SEM = 0.15 ± 0.04, CI = 0.07–0.22, t(29) = 4.05, p < 0.001, d = 0.74) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Suppression durations tended to be shorter in the visuotactile condition than in the congruent visual-only condition in Experiment 2.
source: In addition, suppression durations tended to be shorter in the visuotactile condition than in the congruent visual-only condition (mean difference ± SEM = −0.09 ± 0.04, CI = −0.18–0.00, t(29) = −1.94, p = 0.063, d = 0.37).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: These differences in percept durations were not observed between the incongruent conditions in Experiment 2.
source: Importantly, these differences were not observed between the incongruent conditions (hand percept: mean difference ± SEM = 0.00 ± 0.04, CI = −0.08–0.08, t(29) = −0.01, p = 0.994, d = 0.00; mask percept: mean difference ± SEM = −0.02 ± 0.08, CI = −0.18–0.14, t(29) = −0.23, p = 0.803, d = 0.06).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Only when the hand image was congruent with the participant's real hand did visuotactile stimulation lead to changes in percept durations.
source: Thus, only when the hand image was congruent with the participant's real hand did visuotactile stimulation lead to changes in percept durations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the percept duration analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: It is ownership of the hand, not synchronous visuotactile stimulation, that causes changes in binocular rivalry dynamics.
source: This result is consistent with our hypothesis that it is ownership of the hand, not synchronous visuotactile stimulation, that causes these changes in binocular rivalry dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 2.

claim: Across experiments, the congruent visuotactile condition yielded longer hand-percept durations and shorter mask-percept durations than the congruent visual-only condition.
source: Across experiments, the congruent visuotactile condition, in which participants experienced ownership of the hand image, yielded longer hand-percept durations and shorter mask-percept durations than the congruent visual-only condition (hand percept: mean difference ± SEM = 0.14 ± 0.03, CI = 0.07–0.21, t(59) = 4.06, p < 0.001, d = 0.62; mask percept: mean difference ± SEM = 0.09 ± 0.04, CI = 0.02–0.17, t(59) = −2.50, p = 0.015, d = 0.32) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the combined analysis of both experiments.

claim: Individual touches affected the overall dominance of the hand image in the congruent conditions of Experiment 2.
source: As in Experiment 1, we found that individual touches affected the overall dominance of the hand image in the congruent conditions, that is, we found a main effect of time during the period surrounding a touch (visuotactile: F(5,145) = 32.66, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.53; visual-only: F(5,145) = 51.17, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.64).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the time-course analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: For both incongruent conditions in Experiment 2, there was a strong effect of time during the period surrounding a touch.
source: Indeed, for both conditions, we found a strong effect of time during the period surrounding a touch (visuotactile: F(5,145) = 27.71, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.49; visual-only: F(5,145) = 34.75, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.55).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the time-course analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Whenever there is movement of the stick, the probability of perceiving the hand image increases.
source: Together, these results show that whenever there is movement of the stick, the probability of perceiving the hand image increases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-course analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Individual touches did not affect the difference between visuotactile and visual-only for the congruent conditions in Experiment 2.
source: Individual touches did not affect the difference between visuotactile and visual-only for the congruent conditions (F(5,145) = 0.86, p = 0.51, η2 = 0.03) (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the time-course analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The effect of visuotactile stimulation on hand dominance does not appear to be caused by individual touches.
source: Thus, as in Experiment 1, the effect of visuotactile stimulation on hand dominance does not appear to be caused by individual touches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-course analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The results are more consistent with a continuous effect of ownership of the hand.
source: Instead, the results are more consistent with a continuous effect of ownership of the hand.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the time-course analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: In both experiments, the interaction effect seemed to decrease upon single touches.
source: In both experiments, the interaction effect seemed to decrease upon single touches, probably because the effects of seeing the moving object (and perhaps that of tactile stimulation) set in, reducing the relative effect of ownership.
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation from the time-course analysis.

claim: The continuous effect that was independent of single touches was most likely caused by the continuous presence of ownership in the congruent visuotactile condition.
source: In the congruent visuotactile condition, the continuous effect that was independent of single touches was most likely caused by the continuous presence of ownership in these conditions, which was independent of single touches.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the time-course analysis.

claim: Overall, maintaining a hand percept was more likely in the congruent visuotactile condition than in the congruent visual-only condition in Experiment 2.
source: We found that, overall, maintaining a hand percept was more likely in the congruent visuotactile condition than in the congruent visual-only condition (F(1,29) = 12.05, p = 0.002, η2 = 0.29) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the single percept analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The likelihood of maintaining the hand percept was higher in the congruent visuotactile condition than in the congruent visual-only condition, but this effect did not depend on single touches in Experiment 2.
source: Thus, as in Experiment 1, the likelihood of maintaining the hand percept was higher in the congruent visuotactile condition than in the congruent visual-only condition, but this effect did not depend on single touches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single percept analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The difference between the congruent visuotactile condition and the congruent visual-only condition in switching probability was significantly greater during touch in Experiment 2.
source: Interestingly, although the overall higher switching probability in the congruent visuotactile condition did not reach significance (F(1,29) = 2.48, p = 0.126, η2 = 0.08), we found that the difference between the congruent visuotactile condition and the congruent visual-only condition was significantly greater during touch (F(1,29) = 4.34, p = 0.046, η2 = 0.13)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the single percept analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Individual touches increased the likelihood of the hand percept breaking through suppression, but only in the visuotactile condition, in which ownership was present.
source: Thus, individual touches increased the likelihood of the hand percept breaking through suppression, but only in the visuotactile condition, in which ownership was present.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single percept analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: These effects on maintaining and switching percepts were not found in the incongruent conditions of Experiment 2.
source: Importantly, these effects were not found in the incongruent conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single percept analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The longer maintenance of hand percepts was caused not by single touches but by a sustained effect of ownership of the hand (combined analysis).
source: Together, these analyses show that the longer maintenance of hand percepts was caused not by single touches but by a sustained effect of ownership of the hand.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined analysis of both experiments.

claim: Recovering the hand from suppression does appear to rely on single touches, but only in the specific condition in which ownership of the hand is experimentally induced (combined analysis).
source: In contrast, recovering the hand from suppression does appear to rely on single touches, but only in the specific condition in which ownership of the hand is experimentally induced, that is, the congruent visuotactile condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined analysis of both experiments.

claim: Even though the hand percept is suppressed, some information about ownership of the hand is maintained.
source: Interestingly, this suggests that even though the hand percept is suppressed, some information about ownership of the hand is maintained.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the finding about recovery from suppression.

claim: In the presence of body ownership, the overall perceptual dominance of a hand increased in binocular rivalry.
source: A key finding was that in the presence of body ownership, the overall perceptual dominance of that hand increased.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: Participants who reported stronger ownership also had a greater effect of visuotactile stimulation on the dominance of the hand image.
source: Interestingly, participants who reported stronger ownership also had a greater effect of visuotactile stimulation on the dominance of that hand image.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Mere tactile stimulation of each participant's real hand without induction of ownership did not increase the dominance of the hand image.
source: Moreover, mere tactile stimulation of each participant's real hand without induction of ownership (tactile-only condition) did not increase the dominance of the hand image.
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 1.

claim: It is body ownership, rather than mere synchronous visuotactile stimulation, that increases the dominance of the hand image.
source: Together, these results suggest that it is body ownership, rather than mere synchronous visuotactile stimulation, that increases the dominance of the hand image.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The dominance increase correlated positively with participants' individual ownership illusion score.
source: Crucially, in both experiments, we found that this dominance increase correlated positively with participants' individual ownership illusion score.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis across both experiments.

claim: The effects of ownership on dominance were greatest before the onset of single touches, in agreement with the interpretation that it is sustained ownership of the hand that drives the dominance effect.
source: Moreover, these effects were greatest before the onset of single touches, in agreement with the interpretation that it is sustained ownership of the hand that drives the dominance effect rather than transient visuotactile events.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-course analysis.

claim: The finding that ownership promotes visual awareness provides an important new role for ownership in sensory processing.
source: The finding that ownership promotes visual awareness provides an important new role for ownership in sensory processing and helps to explain the central role of body ownership in conscious awareness.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim about the significance of the findings.

claim: Ownership can change the content of conscious perception by enhancing tactile acuity.
source: We know from earlier studies that ownership can change the content of conscious perception in such ways as enhancing tactile acuity (Haggard et al., 2003; Longo et al., 2008)
evidence: This is a claim about prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Ownership can calibrate proprioception.
source: calibrating proprioception (Abdulkarim and Ehrsson, 2016; Botvinick and Cohen, 1998; Tsakiris and Haggard, 2005)
evidence: This is a claim about prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Ownership can scale visuospatial perception.
source: and scaling visuospatial perception (van der Hoort and Ehrsson, 2014, van der Hoort and Ehrsson, 2016; van der Hoort et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a claim about prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Body ownership can affect the very presence of conscious perception, namely, visual awareness.
source: The fundamental advance made in this study is the demonstration that body ownership can affect the very presence of conscious perception, namely, visual awareness.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the current study's findings.

claim: An increase in overall dominance can be caused by longer dominance durations or by shorter suppression durations.
source: An increase in overall dominance can be caused by longer dominance durations or by shorter suppression durations.
evidence: This is a statement about binocular rivalry mechanisms.

claim: Dominance and suppression rely on distinct neural processes.
source: It is important to distinguish between the two because dominance and suppression rely on distinct neural processes (Blake and Logothetis, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about binocular rivalry, supported by citation.

claim: Ownership increased the durations of individual hand percepts and decreased the durations of suppression.
source: We found evidence for both: ownership increased the durations of individual hand percepts and decreased the durations of suppression.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The hand percepts were maintained longer independently of individual visuotactile events.
source: The hand percepts were maintained longer independently of individual visuotactile events.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-course analysis.

claim: The effect of ownership on hand percept duration cannot be explained by increased voluntary attention toward the hand image.
source: This effect cannot be explained by increased voluntary attention toward the hand image for two reasons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: There was no difference in switch rate between conditions with identical visual input, suggesting that the overall attentional demand is the same between conditions.
source: First, we did not find a difference in switch rate between conditions with identical visual input, suggesting that the overall attentional demand is the same between conditions (Paffen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the switch rate analysis, supported by citation.

claim: The effect of ownership on suppression durations, which is not affected by voluntary attention, was of similar magnitude to the effect of ownership on dominance durations.
source: Second, the effect of ownership on suppression durations, which is not affected by voluntary attention (Ooi and He, 1999; Paffen and Alais, 2011), was of similar magnitude to the effect of ownership on dominance durations.
evidence: This is a finding from the percept duration analysis, supported by citations.

claim: The prolonged dominance suggests that ownership effectively increases the 'stimulus strength' of the visual hand stimulus, similar to an increase in contrast.
source: Instead, the prolonged dominance suggests that ownership effectively increases the 'stimulus strength' of the visual hand stimulus, similar to an increase in contrast (Brascamp et al., 2015), and thereby prevents the suppressed mask stimulus from entering the subject's awareness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: The decreased suppression durations seemed to be driven by single visuotactile events, but only when there was ownership of the suppressed hand.
source: In contrast to prolonged dominance, the decreased suppression durations seemed to be driven by single visuotactile events, but only when there was ownership of the suppressed hand.
evidence: This is a finding from the single percept analysis.

claim: Traces of the suppressed hand stimulus still contain information about ownership.
source: This result suggests that traces of the suppressed hand stimulus still contain information about ownership and that these traces are perceptually bound to the tactile stimulus in the case of ownership in order to break through suppression.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Hand ownership arises from multisensory integration in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) and the premotor cortex.
source: Hand ownership is known to arise from multisensory integration in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) and the premotor cortex (Ehrsson, 2012; Ehrsson et al., 2004; Gentile et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the neural basis of hand ownership, supported by citations.

claim: Visual perception of hand images occurs in a part of the lateral occipital complex (LOC) known as the extrastriate body area (EBA).
source: Visual perception of hand images occurs in a part of the lateral occipital complex (LOC) known as the extrastriate body area (EBA) (Downing et al., 2001)
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual processing of body parts, supported by citation.

claim: The EBA is able to dissociate between the visual impressions of one's own hand and someone else's hand.
source: which is additionally able to dissociate between the visual impressions of one's own hand and someone else's hand (Myers and Sowden, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the EBA, supported by citation.

claim: During hand-ownership illusions, the LOC/EBA is activated.
source: During hand-ownership illusions, the LOC/EBA is activated (Gentile et al., 2013; Limanowski et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a finding from prior neuroimaging research, supported by citations.

claim: The effective connectivity between the LOC/EBA and the IPS is increased during hand-ownership illusions.
source: and the effective connectivity between this area and the IPS is increased, indicating increases in neural communication between the two regions (Gentile et al., 2013; Guterstam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from prior neuroimaging research, supported by citations.

claim: Functional connectivity between the IPS and the EBA increases the strength of the visual hand stimulus, thereby resulting in longer dominance durations of that hand.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that functional connectivity between the IPS and the EBA increases the strength of the visual hand stimulus, thereby resulting in longer dominance durations of that hand.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the neural mechanism underlying the findings.

claim: During instances of suppression, traces of the suppressed hand image may travel along the dorsal stream and reach the IPS, as is the case for suppressed images of tools.
source: During instances of suppression, traces of the suppressed hand image may travel along the dorsal stream and reach the IPS, as is the case for suppressed images of tools (Fang and He, 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Signals related to the suppressed hand image would integrate with spatiotemporally congruent signals associated with the tactile stimulus in the IPS and consequently increase the signal-to-noise ratio of the hand image in the EBA.
source: Here, signals related to this suppressed hand image would integrate with spatiotemporally congruent signals associated with the tactile stimulus and consequently increase the signal-to-noise ratio of the hand image in the EBA, increase its inhibition of signals related to the dominant mask percept, and thereby speed up its recovery from suppression.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the neural mechanism.

claim: The results cannot distinguish between whether body ownership boosts visual awareness 'directly' at the higher level of conscious selection, or if body ownership influences visual awareness 'indirectly' by first increasing the signal strength in lower level visual representations.
source: Our results cannot distinguish between these two alternatives.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in interpreting the findings.

claim: Invisible stimulus features can induce binocular rivalry.
source: We know from a recent study by Zou et al. (2016) that invisible stimulus features can induce binocular rivalry, which shows that the subjective perceptual alternation in this paradigm can be influenced by signal processing at early stages of visual processing.
evidence: This is a finding from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Body ownership illusions are associated with multisensory integration in fronto-parietal association cortices.
source: Body ownership illusions on the other hand are associated with multisensory integration in fronto-parietal association cortices (Ehrsson et al., 2004; Gentile et al., 2013; Limanowski and Blankenburg, 2016; Petkova et al., 2011; Preston and Ehrsson, 2016)
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Fronto-parietal association cortices are implied in theories of consciousness such as the Global Work Space theory.
source: – brain regions that are also implied in theories of consciousness such as the Global Work Space theory (Dehaene and Naccache, 2001; Lau and Rosenthal, 2011)
evidence: This is a statement about theories of consciousness, supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that ownership influences its effects at the higher level of conscious selection.
source: so it is possible that ownership influences its effects at this higher level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism.

claim: The interpretation that body ownership could influence visual processing of the hand image in lower level representations by increasing its signal strength fits well with the recurrent processing theory of consciousness.
source: However, it should be pointed out that this account also fits well with the recurrent processing theory of consciousness (Lamme, 2006), which claims that awareness is the result of recurrent processing.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation, supported by citation.

claim: According to the recurrent processing theory, body ownership could increase recurrent processing from the IPS to the EBA, and thereby 'directly' increase visual awareness of the hand image.
source: According to this theory body ownership could increase recurrent processing from the IPS to the EBA, and thereby 'directly' increase visual awareness of the hand image.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on the recurrent processing theory.

claim: The possible existence of a direct causal relationship between body ownership and conscious awareness remains to be clarified in future studies.
source: Thus, although our results clearly show that body ownership increases the subjective dominance of the hand image, the possible existence of a direct causal relationship between body ownership and conscious awareness remains to be clarified in future studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations and future directions of the research.

claim: The dynamics of binocular rivalry is affected by nonvisual stimuli that are congruent to one of the rival images.
source: Previous studies have extensively shown that the dynamics of binocular rivalry is affected by nonvisual stimuli that are congruent to one of the rival images.
evidence: This is a summary of prior research findings.

claim: Nonvisual stimuli affecting binocular rivalry can be tactile, auditory, and even olfactory in nature.
source: These nonvisual stimuli can be tactile (Lunghi and Alais, 2013; Lunghi et al., 2010), auditory (Conrad et al., 2010; Sekuler et al., 1997), and even olfactory (Zhou et al., 2010) in nature.
evidence: This is a summary of prior research findings, supported by citations.

claim: The current findings differ from earlier findings in that rivalry dynamics were altered by ownership specifically and not tactile stimulation in general.
source: However, although we used tactile stimulation to induce ownership, the current findings differ from these earlier findings in that rivalry dynamics were altered by ownership specifically and not tactile stimulation in general.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to prior research.

claim: Ownership itself does not belong to a single sensory modality but arises when visual, tactile, and proprioceptive information are congruent and can be perceptually bound.
source: Ownership itself does not belong to a single sensory modality but arises when visual, tactile, and proprioceptive information are congruent and can be perceptually bound.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the nature of ownership.

claim: The effects of tactile stimulation on binocular rivalry have been attributed mainly to visuotactile interactions occurring at lower levels of visual processing.
source: Another difference in the effects of tactile stimulation is that these effects have been attributed mainly to visuotactile interactions occurring at lower levels of visual processing (Lunghi et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a statement about prior research findings, supported by citation.

claim: The effect of ownership seems more likely to occur in the IPS and EBA.
source: whereas the effect of ownership seems more likely to occur in the IPS and EBA (Gentile et al., 2013; Guterstam et al., 2013; Limanowski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the neural mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The ownership illusion used in this binocular study is different from the classic rubber-hand illusion in several aspects.
source: The ownership illusion used in this binocular study is different from the classic rubber-hand illusion (Botvinick and Cohen, 1998) in several aspects.
evidence: This is a statement comparing the current methodology to prior work.

claim: The hand was presented to only one eye, and therefore perception of the hand was two-dimensional.
source: First, the hand was presented to only one eye, and therefore perception of the hand was two-dimensional.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: The image of the hand was considerably smaller than a life-sized rubber hand.
source: Second, the image of the hand was considerably smaller than a life-sized rubber hand.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Larger rival images tend to render more mixed-percept states.
source: The reason for this was that larger rival images tend to render more mixed-percept states, and we aimed to achieve rivalry dynamics that would make which percept was dominant less ambiguous to reduce response biases.
evidence: This is a statement about binocular rivalry methodology.

claim: Both the hand's small size and its two-dimensional nature may have caused the ownership illusion to be weakened compared with a classical rubber-hand illusion.
source: Both the hand's small size (Pavani and Zampini, 2007) and its two-dimensional nature (IJsselsteijn et al., 2006) may have caused the ownership illusion to be weakened compared with a classical rubber-hand illusion.
evidence: This is a speculation about the strength of the illusion, supported by citations.

claim: The results of the questionnaire data demonstrated that a relatively strong limb-ownership illusion was elicited, with affirmative ratings of ownership that were comparable to those from previous studies with actual rubber hands.
source: However, the results of our questionnaire data demonstrated that we elicited a relatively strong limb-ownership illusion, with affirmative ratings of ownership that were comparable to those from previous studies with actual rubber hands (Kalckert and Ehrsson, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current results to prior research, supported by citation.

claim: One can speculate that ownership of one's real hand should have an even larger effect on visual awareness than the experimental design allowed for.
source: Nevertheless, one can speculate that ownership of one's real hand should have an even larger effect on visual awareness than our experimental design allowed for.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential magnitude of the effect.

claim: Visuoproprioceptive congruency between the participant's real hand and the hand image in the absence of any dynamic tactile stimulation did not affect the rivalry dynamics of the hand image.
source: First, in each experiment, we included two conditions that differed only in terms of the visuoproprioceptive congruency between the participant's real hand and the hand image in the absence of any dynamic tactile stimulation, and we found that this methodology did not affect the rivalry dynamics of the hand image.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from both experiments.

claim: Visuospatial congruency of the seen and felt position of the hand did not overcome suppression of that hand.
source: Thus, visuospatial congruency of the seen and felt position of the hand did not overcome suppression of that hand.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: A hand image that was congruent with the participant's hand recovered from suppression slightly faster (60 ms) than a hand image that was incongruent to the participant's real hand in a continuous flash suppression experiment.
source: This result seems to be in conflict with a recent continuous flash suppression experiment (Salomon et al., 2013) indicating that a hand image that was congruent with the participant's hand recovered from suppression slightly faster (60 ms) than a hand image that was incongruent to the participant's real hand.
evidence: This is a finding from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Binocular rivalry might be less sensitive to small changes in suppression durations than continuous flash suppression.
source: However, in the current study, we used binocular rivalry, which might be less sensitive to such small changes in suppression durations.
evidence: This is a speculation about methodological differences.

claim: As soon as the moving object started to move, the dominance of the hand image increased.
source: A second interesting observation comes from the analysis of the visual-only conditions in which the moving object (ball on a stick) was visible at all times because it was part of both images. As soon as this object started to move, the dominance of the hand image increased.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-course analysis.

claim: Visuospatial context is known to affect binocular rivalry.
source: Because visuospatial context is known to affect binocular rivalry (Alais and Blake, 1999), this result indicates that the hand image provides a better context for the moving object than the mask image.
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: The hand image provides a better context for the moving object than the mask image.
source: Because visuospatial context is known to affect binocular rivalry (Alais and Blake, 1999), this result indicates that the hand image provides a better context for the moving object than the mask image.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: This is the first example of a contextual effect in binocular rivalry that is specific to movement.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first example of a contextual effect in binocular rivalry that is specific to movement.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: The hand image probably provides a more congruent visual context because it has similar depth cues for the moving stick and because it is a more ecological visual stimulus than the mask image.
source: The hand image probably provides a more congruent visual context because it has similar depth cues (e.g., shadow and visual perspective) for the moving stick and because it is a more ecological visual stimulus than the mask image.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the contextual effect.

claim: Movement close to a hand is a strong cue for stimulation in peripersonal space, a stimulus that activates visuotactile neuronal populations in the fronto-parietal association cortices.
source: We speculate that this finding relates to movement close to a hand being a strong cue for stimulation in peripersonal space, a stimulus that activates visuotactile neuronal populations in the fronto-parietal association cortices (Brozzoli et al., 2011; Fogassi et al., 1996; Graziano et al., 1997; Makin et al., 2007), including those with mirror-neuron properties (Brozzoli et al., 2013; Ishida et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation about the neural mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: Ownership of a hand increases the visual awareness of that hand, both by increasing the strength of the hand-image and by overcoming suppression when the hand is being touched.
source: Together, the results of this study suggest that ownership of a hand increases the visual awareness of that hand, both by increasing the strength of the hand-image, as if it increases in contrast, and by overcoming suppression when the hand is being touched.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: These findings increase the understanding of the role of ownership in visual perception in that ownership seems to enhance visual processing of a body part that is ours because it is more relevant to us, especially when it is being touched by an external source.
source: These findings increase the understanding of the role of ownership in visual perception in that ownership seems to enhance visual processing of a body part that is ours because it is more relevant to us, especially when it is being touched by an external source.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim about the significance of the findings.
